subject: Weird predicted values from a distamp model

messages.author: b0084e74319ebcb3
messages.subject: Weird predicted values from a distamp model
parts:
Hello everyone,

Recently I asked if using backTransform is necessary before using predict to handle models constructed using distsamp. Reading previous posts I realize that I can just use predict, and not use backTransform but I am getting strange results. I have fitted several models using distsamp that includes categorical and continuous variables. I choose the best model for my data based on Akaike weights and now I am want to plot the results. The selected model has one categorical (habitat type, four categories) and one continuous site covariate (elevation) . Then I used the predict function , but I am getting very strange results when I predict for different values of elevation (continuous variable) keeping habitat constant (continuous variable). I get almost a straight line with negative slope, and I know from my raw data that the abundance at sites with very low elevation is extremely low (is almost 0). The results look really strange. Anybody know what can be happening? Below some of my code and results and attached the graph of the results:

#This is the best fit model that includes two variables explaining the state. I already try to use the other "keyfun" and results are consistent. I also checked the goodness of fit.
EH <- distsamp(~1~Elevation_meters+Updated_Habitat,  data, keyfun = "hazard")

#Data frame keeping habitat type constant. What I want is to see how abundance changes with elevation. This are the results that seem weird
habConst <-data.frame(Elevation_meters=seq(500,3500,length=20),Updated_Habitat=factor("Primary_forest",levels=unique(c$Updated_Habitat)))
pHabCost <-predict (EH,type="state",newdata=habConst,appendData=TRUE)

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Weird predicted values from a distamp model
parts:
The model coefficient suggests a negative linear relationship between density and elevation.  Have you tried adding a quadratic effect?  Straight linear relationships with environmental gradients are sometimes not reasonable.

I would also suggest scaling your elevation values (km instead of m) and/or standardizing them.

messages.author: b0084e74319ebcb3
messages.subject: Re: Weird predicted values from a distamp model
parts:
Hello everyone,

Just to post the solution of my problem. Thanks to the help of Dan Linden I figured most of things out. The main problem that I had is that I was only fitting models with linear relationships between elevation and abundance. So I fit quadratic models, the AIC values are lower and the results actually make sense! Also, when fitting this models I used the scale function. 

The selected model still includes one categorical and one continuous variable, and now I am having problems with the prediction for the categorical variable. But I will leave that for another post...

Best,

Laura
